#| include: false

The dataset available at <https://uoepsy.github.io/data/social_media.csv> contains data on social media use and sleep quality for a random sample of UK university students. The following variables are included:

- `screen_time`: Hours spent on social media per day (continuous)
- `sleep_quality`: Self-reported sleep quality score (out of 100, continuous)

Before you start answering any questions, read the data into R.

Using a 5% significance level, you will answer the following research question: 

> Is there a linear relationship between the number of hours spent on social media per day and self-reported sleep quality scores among university students?


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q1 given RQ, choose appropriate test -->

Which of the following statistical tests is the most appropriate to answer the research question? Discuss within your group and write in your R script your choice and why using comments (`#`).

1. Independent samples t-test  
2. One-sample t-test  
3. Pearson's correlation  
4. Chi-squared test of independence

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`
Based on the variable types, we would choose 3. Pearson's correlation. Both variables (`screen_time` and `sleep_quality`) are continuous numeric variables, and we are interested in the strength and direction of their linear relationship.

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q2 run test (pearson's cor) -->

Run the test in R. Both correlation and hypothesis test should be done as part of this question.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

- Use the `cor.test()` function, with the default argument `method = "pearson"`.

- The correlation is given by the part `sample estimates` of the output. Or you can compute it directly with the `cor()` function but this doesn't give you the hypothesis test.

:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
social_media <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/social_media.csv")

cor_res <- cor.test(social_media$screen_time, social_media$sleep_quality)
cor_res
```

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q3 check assumptions -->

Check if the data requirements / assumptions of Pearson's correlation are met.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

1. Continuous variables. Both variables should be continuous.

2. No extreme outliers. There should be no data points that are far away from the others.

3. Linearity assumption. Create a scatterplot of `screen_time` (x-axis) and `sleep_quality` (y-axis) with a linear trend line (`geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE)`) and LOESS curve (`geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = FALSE)`). If the relationship is linear the two lines should roughly match.

4. Normality assumption. Check if each variable is roughly normally distributed using QQ-plots (`... + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()`) or Shapiro-Wilk tests (`shapiro.test()`)

5. Equal variance assumption. Check the plot for linearity to see if each variable's variance is equal across the range of the other variable.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

1. Both variables are numeric and continuous, so this data requirement is met.

2. The scatterplot shows no data points that are very far away from the others.

```{r}
ggplot(social_media, aes(x = screen_time, y = sleep_quality)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Daily Screen Time (hours)", y = "Sleep Quality Score (0-100)")
```


3. The code below adds a solid blue straight line and a dashed red LOESS curve to the scatterplot:

```{r}
ggplot(social_media, aes(x = screen_time, y = sleep_quality)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, colour = 'blue') +
  geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = FALSE, colour = 'red', linetype = 'dashed') +
  labs(x = "Daily Screen Time (hours)", y = "Sleep Quality Score (0-100)")
```

The scatterplot shows a negative linear trend, i.e. the points have a decreasing trend where as daily screen time tends to increase, sleep quality tends to decrease. There LOESS curve and straight line are close enough to indicate linearity.


4. Normality.

```{r}
# QQ-plots
screen_plt <- ggplot(social_media, aes(sample = screen_time)) +
  geom_qq() + 
  geom_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles",
       title = "Screen time QQplot")

sleep_plt <- ggplot(social_media, aes(sample = sleep_quality)) +
  geom_qq() + 
  geom_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles",
       title = "Sleep quality QQplot")

# Load the patchwork library to put plots side by side using +
library(patchwork)
screen_plt + sleep_plt

# Shapiro-Wilk tests
shapiro.test(social_media$screen_time)
shapiro.test(social_media$sleep_quality)
```

The Shapiro-Wilk tests for `screen_time` and `sleep_quality` give $p$-values of .26 and .69 respectively (both $> .05$), indicating that we do not reject the null hypothesis of normality. The QQ-plots also show good agreement between the sample quantiles and theoretical quantiles. The assumption of normality for Pearson's correlation is therefore met.

5. Equal variance. Looking the linearity plot from (3), we can see that the spread of the points is roughly constant as we move along the x-axis, so this assumption is also met.

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q4 find cohen's D effect size -->

For Pearson correlations, the correlation coefficient ($r$) itself is the effect size.

Find the $r$ value from your `cor.test` output (or calculate it using `cor()`).

Based on the lecture recommendations (copied below), how would you interpret the magnitude and direction of this effect? What does this mean in context of the study?

| Effect Size | Magnitude |
|:------------|:----------|
| Weak        | .1 to .3  |
| Moderate    | .3 to .5  |
| Strong      | >.5       |

`r qend()`

`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
# Extracting r
pearson_cor <- cor(social_media$screen_time, social_media$sleep_quality)
pearson_cor
```

The correlation coefficient is $r$ = -.57.

Because the absolute value (`r round(abs(pearson_cor), 2)`) is greater than .5, this represents a strong effect. The negative sign tells us the direction, i.e. as screen time increased, sleep quality tended to decrease.

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q5 write up / report -->

Let's practice how to report the results of your correlation test in APA style.

Write a brief summary of your results, making sure to include:

- The research question
- The sample size
- The test statistic ($t$), degrees of freedom ($df$), $p$-value, and correlation.
- The effect size ($r$) and its interpretation

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

You can follow this structure: 

> A [test name] was conducted to examine [research question]. There was a [strength and direction] relationship between [variable1] and [variable2], $t(df)$ = [value], $p$ [value], $r$ = [value]. [User-friendly conclusion]. 

:::

`r qend()`

`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

> A Pearson correlation test was conducted to examine the relationship between daily screen time and sleep quality scores in a sample of UK university students ($N$ = 85). There was a strong, negative linear relationship between the two variables, $t$(83) = -6.33, $p$ < .001, $r$ = -.57. As daily screen time increased, sleep quality scores tended to significantly decrease.

`r solend()`
